overview: The Ahantchuyuk, also called the Pudding River or French Prairie people, were a Kalapuya community in Oregon’s Willamette Valley. Champoeg connected their food gathering, travel and exchange with neighbouring peoples.

periods.title: Land cession and promised support
periods.summary: The 1855 Willamette Valley treaty ceded land to the United States and required removal to a designated home, in exchange for promised payments and services.

periods.title: Removal and reservation life
periods.summary: Removal brought Ahantchuyuk people to Grand Ronde. The March 1856 reservation ledger records the French Prairie band among the newly assembled communities.

periods.title: Federal termination and community persistence
periods.summary: Congress ended Grand Ronde’s federal recognition in 1954. Family connections continued through the loss of federal status and the campaign to regain recognition.

periods.title: Restored recognition and rebuilding
periods.summary: The Grand Ronde Restoration Act became law in 1983. The Confederated Tribes rebuilt institutions and services after restoration.

periods.title: Teaching living traditions
periods.summary: Grand Ronde’s Lifeways program began in 2005, connecting members with the lands and practices of the confederation’s constituent communities.

items.text: Families moved seasonally between food sources, including camas prairies and acorn-gathering areas. Yampah grew near Champoeg. David Lewis’s reconstruction also describes trade for preserved salmon and lamprey at the falls. Food knowledge included storage and exchange as well as knowing when and where to gather.

Alexander Henry’s January 1814 account describes local hunters wearing a deer’s head and imitating the animal’s movements to approach deer. Lewis places this observation in Ahantchuyuk country. It records skill in reading animal behaviour, but remains a visitor’s account of a particular encounter rather than a complete description of every hunt.

Grand Ronde Elder Greg Archuleta explains that Kalapuya cooks baked camas bulbs, mashed them into cakes and dried them for storage and trade. Prolonged cooking changes the bulbs’ inulin. This account connects food processing with portable provisions; it describes a broader Kalapuya practice rather than an excavated Ahantchuyuk household.

Archuleta’s account also connects plant management with basketry: flexible hazel supplied useful material, while seed fans and baskets helped harvest tarweed. Such technologies depended on selecting suitable plants and maintaining productive gathering places. The account concerns regional traditions and does not establish identical methods in every village.

sections.title: What records preserve and leave out

items.text: The Grand Ronde Reservation log book, catalogued as Mss555_F3, includes a March 1856 census naming the French Prairie band. It lists household heads and family sizes alongside other communities. This is concrete evidence of people living after removal, not support for treating the map’s 1500 endpoint as their disappearance.

The same volume records supplies issued to arriving households and property left by earlier settlers. These accounts reveal the administrative organization of reservation life. Their scope is limited: a government distribution ledger cannot by itself describe all household food, possessions, work or continuing cultural practices.

The 1855 treaty text promises payments, clothing, provisions, tools and agricultural support, with a physician, teacher and blacksmith after removal. Reading its clauses shows what the United States undertook to provide. The promises should be distinguished from what families actually received and from their own existing skills.

The treaty also allowed land to be divided into household allotments and tied continued possession to residence and cultivation. These provisions sought to reorganize land use and work under federal supervision. They help explain why removal meant a transformation of institutions as well as a change of location.

Grand Ronde families remained connected after termination. Tribal leaders organized, raised funds and testified before Congress to restore federal recognition, achieved in 1983. This was the work of the wider confederation, within which Ahantchuyuk history continues. The campaign restored legal recognition of an existing community.

Yampah has been restored at Champoeg with Tribal input, according to Archuleta’s public account. Restoring an important food plant makes the site more than a monument to settler government. It connects a named place with continuing knowledge about the plants that supported its earlier community.

The Lifeways program offers cultural classes that recognize the different tribes and bands within Grand Ronde. Reconnecting people with particular homelands and practices is an achievement in teaching and community life. The confederation’s shared institutions do not require every constituent history to be treated as identical.

ending.text: Removal to Grand Ronde transformed Ahantchuyuk community life. Their history continues within the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde. Federal termination in 1954 ended recognition, not the people; recognition was restored in 1983. No historical disappearance in 1500 is established by the map.
